description: Galvanised tapered steel street lighting column with a single curved outreach arm and a cobra-head lantern

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall galvanised steel street lighting column standing complete and upright with its whole length in frame from the ground to the top, octagonal in section and tapering as it rises from a wide square bolted base flange, a flat rectangular access door plate low on the shaft, and at the top the column bending over into one long smooth curved outreach arm that sweeps sideways well clear of the shaft and levels out horizontally, carrying on its far end a closed cobra-head lantern housing shaped as a broad wedge that is deep where it meets the arm and tapers to a shallow rounded nose, its underside a single flat clear lens panel. The lantern sits out to one side on the end of the arm, never directly on top of the column Materials: Hot-dip galvanised steel gone dull matt grey with white zinc bloom, running rust streaks below the access door and around the base bolts, road grime and splash darkening the lowest metre, grey painted lantern housing chalky on its sunward side, insect debris behind the lens.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless pure WHITE studio matte. The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless white backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient. This is a studio cut-out, NOT an outdoor photograph: there must be no sky, no clouds, no buildings, no road and no overhead cables anywhere in the frame.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo. The lamp is switched OFF and emits no light.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 2.61 x 8.85 x 0.34 m. Cost: 1104 triangles / 16000, 4 draw calls / 12, 3 materials / 8, 4 unique geometries / 16, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.758, 1.0, 0.97], interior hole fractions [0.0014, 0.0051, 0.0021, 0.0001]).  Four components at 4 draw calls and 3 materials, which is the structure this asset's own quality contract requires (>=2 macro, >=2 meso, >=3 material layers); a single merged mesh would have been cheaper for a prop placed in runs of twenty but fails that contract.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 2.61 x 8.85 x 0.34 m against the declared 2.6 x 9 x 0.36 -- within 2% on every axis. The proportions come from the DECLARATION and not from the plate, deliberately: silh.mjs profiles the plate's shaft at 0.0735 of its own height where a 9 m column with the declared 0.2 m shaft is 0.022, so the plate is a short car-park lamp, stubbier by 3.3x, and its arm reach reads 0.63 of height against the declared 0.28. Scaling this prop off its plate would have produced a 9 m column with a 0.66 m shaft.

An EASED quarter-turn -- tight at the top, straight along the outreach -- rather than a circular arc, which is the shape of a real bracket arm and what the plate shows. The tube leaves the shaft at 7.30 m, runs horizontal at 8.72 m and reaches 1.73 m from the axis, putting the luminaire's nose at 2.43 m and the measured width at the declared 2.6 with the baseplate. A circular arc would bulge into the carriageway at mid-height and land the head short.

A 0.70 m cast wedge, deepest at the spigot (0.150 m) and tapering to the nose (0.086 m) over an acrylic refractor bowl hung proud of the casting's underside. A plain box reads as a shoebox on a stick; the taper is the cobra. Sized from the plate at 2.7 shaft-widths. Against the plate the head still reads small, and that is the declaration's doing rather than a modelling error -- a 0.70 m luminaire on a 9 m column is proportionally correct and the plate's lamp is 3.3x stubbier.

A 12-segment lathe tapering r 0.105 to 0.072 over 7.3 m, about 12%, read off the plate's silhouette profile -- and FLARING into the baseplate over the bottom 0.55 m from r 0.158. The previous build was a constant-radius pipe with neither. The swaged collar at 2.20 m, where a column's lower section meets its upper tube, is the other half of what reads as a structural column rather than a pipe at close range.

Three material layers: galvanised steel #98a0a2 measured off the plate's subject mask (p25 121,131,132 / p50 142,150,152 / p75 167,169,168), cast aluminium #a8adad for the luminaire -- lighter and smoother, which is what separates the two in the plate -- and acrylic #d8dcd6 at roughness 0.20 for the refractor. Luma 148 sits well clear of the 55.5-60.5 band that gatecrop's alpha key erases, so this needed no lift, unlike this kit's darker props. What is NOT carried is the plate's heavy directional staining down one face; the bloom-and-rust tile is isotropic, which is why this is 0.90.

A 0.34 m square bolted plate with four bolts inset 50 mm, with the shaft flaring down onto it. The previous build had no baseplate at all. 0.34 m rather than 0.40: at 0.40 the plate pushed the measured bbox to 2.79 m against a declared 2.6. The bolted hand-hole door at 0.95 m, which is where the plate's rust runs from, is on the shaft component rather than here.

name: Steel Cobra-Head Street Lamp

notes:
The standard Thai highway and main-road column. Sized from a 9 m mounting height with a 2.5 m outreach, which is what the arm reach in the width figure is: the shaft itself is only about 0.2 m across at the base. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 9 m height would derive, because a lighting column is a handful of tapered cylinders and one lantern box with almost no silhouette for its height, and a level builder places these in runs of twenty or more down a single road -- hero2x would spend 16k triangles and 12 draw calls per lamp post on geometry nobody can resolve at street level. The plate scaffold pushes against thin forms, so the prompt describes the shaft and arm as continuous chunky volumes and asks for no cabling, brackets or fixings hanging off them. Static: bolted to a foundation, so physics stays disabled. Prompt rewritten 2026-08-30 during the preview-image pass: the original put the arm in a subordinate clause and flux/schnell returned a lantern sitting directly on the column top on two seeds. The fixes are stating the full length is in frame (it was cropping the base) and ending with an explicit negative that the lantern is never on top of the column.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.
